lessons.title: Sets and Venn diagrams
lessons.programRef: O Level Mathematics — Sets: notation, union, intersection, complement, Venn diagrams with two and three sets (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the O Level Mathematics syllabus; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use set notation: element, union, intersection, complement, number of elements.
Represent two or three sets on a Venn diagram.
Solve word problems with a Venn diagram and an unknown x.
reviewNotes: Syllabus references are to be checked against the current Cameroon GCE Board O Level Mathematics syllabus.
Notation for the universal set: U and ξ are both used in textbooks; check which one the GCE Board papers use.

blocks.title: Sets and notation
blocks.md:
A **set** is a well-defined collection of objects called **elements**.

- $x \in A$ means x is an element of A.
- n(A) is the **number of elements** of A.
- The **universal set** U (also written $\xi$) contains every element under discussion.
- The **empty set** $\emptyset$ has no elements.

blocks.title: Union, intersection, complement
blocks.md:
- **Union** $A \cup B$: elements in A **or** in B (or in both).
- **Intersection** $A \cap B$: elements in **both** A and B.
- **Complement** $A'$: elements of U that are **not** in A.
- $A \subset B$ (A is a **subset** of B): every element of A is also in B.

blocks.caption: A Venn diagram with two sets: four regions inside the universal set U.
blocks.alt: A rectangle labelled U containing two overlapping circles A (blue) and B (red). The regions are labelled A only, A ∩ B in the overlap, B only, and neither outside both circles.

blocks.title: Counting formula for two sets
blocks.md: The elements of $A \cap B$ are counted twice in n(A) + n(B), so we subtract them once:
blocks.tex: n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)

blocks.title: Method: Venn diagram word problems
blocks.md:
1. Draw the rectangle U and one circle per set.
2. Fill the **intersection first** (call it x if it is unknown).
3. Fill each « only » region by subtraction, for example 24 − x.
4. Write the number outside the circles (« neither »).
5. Add all the regions, set the sum equal to n(U) and solve for x.

blocks.title: Example 1: listing elements
blocks.statement: U = {1, 2, 3, …, 10}, A = {even numbers} and B = {multiples of 3}. List $A \cap B$ and $A \cup B$, then find n(A').

steps.md: List the sets: A = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10} and B = {3, 6, 9}. Place 6 in the overlap first, then the other elements.
The only element in both sets is 6, so $A \cap B$ = {6}. The union collects every element of A or B once: $A \cup B$ = {2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10}.
A' contains the elements of U that are not even: A' = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9}, so n(A') = 5. Check: n(A) + n(A') = 5 + 5 = 10 = n(U).

blocks.title: Example 2: finding x
blocks.statement: In a class of 40 students in Bamenda, 24 play football (F), 17 play basketball (B) and 5 play neither game. How many students play both games?

steps.md: Let x be the number who play both. Then 24 − x play football only and 17 − x play basketball only.
All the regions add up to the class size:

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Writing 24 in the « football » region when some of those students also play basketball: the « only » region is 24 − x.
- Forgetting the region outside the circles (« neither »).
- Adding n(A) + n(B) without subtracting $n(A \cap B)$.
- Listing an element twice in a union: each element is written once.

items: With three sets A, B and C, a Venn diagram has 8 regions. Always start with the centre region (in all three sets), then the regions in exactly two sets, then the « only » regions.
Venn diagrams are named after the English logician John Venn, who described them in 1880.

exercises.prompt: n(A) = 12, n(B) = 9 and $n(A \cap B)$ = 4. Find $n(A \cup B)$.
exercises.method: Use the counting formula: the 4 common elements must be counted only once.
mistakes: Answering 21 (12 + 9): the common elements have been counted twice.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: U = {1, 2, 3, …, 12}, P = {prime numbers} and Q = {odd numbers}. Which set is $P \cap Q$?
exercises.explanation: P = {2, 3, 5, 7, 11} and Q = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11}. The elements in both are 3, 5, 7 and 11 (2 is prime but even; 1 and 9 are odd but not prime).
exercises.method: List both sets in full, then keep only the elements that appear in both lists.
mistakes: Counting 1 as a prime number: a prime has exactly two factors, and 1 has only one.
Giving the union instead of the intersection.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: U = {whole numbers from 1 to 15} and A = {multiples of 4}. Find n(A').
exercises.explanation: A = {4, 8, 12}, so n(A) = 3. The complement contains the other elements of U: n(A') = 15 − 3 = 12.
mistakes: Answering 3: that is n(A), not n(A').
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: A survey of 50 traders at Mokolo market in Yaoundé shows that 30 sell tomatoes, 26 sell onions and 8 sell neither. How many traders sell both tomatoes and onions?
exercises.explanation: Let x sell both. Then (30 − x) + x + (26 − x) + 8 = 50, so 64 − x = 50 and x = 14. Check: 16 + 14 + 12 + 8 = 50.
exercises.method: Draw a Venn diagram, put x in the intersection, fill the « only » regions by subtraction, then add all regions.
mistakes: Forgetting the 8 traders who sell neither.
Writing 30 and 26 in the « only » regions.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: Which set is represented by the shaded region?
exercises.explanation: The shaded region is inside A but outside B: the elements are in A **and** in B'. This is $A \cap B'$ (« A only »).
exercises.method: For each region ask two questions: is it inside A? is it inside B? « Outside B » means B'.
mistakes: Choosing $A \cup B$ or $A$: the overlap is not shaded, so the elements of B are excluded.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level style

exercises.prompt: In a group of 60 students, 30 like Mathematics (M), 28 like Physics (P) and 25 like Chemistry (C). 10 like M and P, 12 like P and C, 9 like M and C, x like all three subjects and 6 like none of them. (The numbers 10, 12 and 9 include the students who like all three.)
exercises.method: Start with the centre (x), then the « exactly two » regions (10 − x, 12 − x, 9 − x), then the « only » regions, and add all 8 regions.
mistakes: Writing 10 in the M and P region without subtracting x.
Forgetting the 6 students outside the circles.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level Paper 2 style

parts.explanation: $n(M \cup P \cup C) = 30 + 28 + 25 - 10 - 12 - 9 + x = 52 + x$. Adding the 6 who like none: 52 + x + 6 = 60, so **x = 2**.

parts.prompt: How many students like Mathematics only?
How many students like exactly two of the subjects?
parts.explanation: M and P only: 10 − 2 = 8; P and C only: 12 − 2 = 10; M and C only: 9 − 2 = 7. Total: 8 + 10 + 7 = 25.

parts.prompt: How many students like Physics but not Chemistry?
parts.explanation: P only = 28 − 8 − 10 − 2 = 8, plus M and P only = 8. So 8 + 8 = 16. Check of all regions: 13 + 8 + 6 + 8 + 10 + 7 + 2 + 6 = 60.

exercises.prompt: In a quarter of Buea, 45 households were surveyed. 28 have a television (T), 20 have a fridge (F), x have both and 7 have neither.
exercises.method: Draw the Venn diagram with x in the intersection, 28 − x and 20 − x in the « only » regions and 7 outside.
mistakes: Forgetting the 7 households with neither appliance.
Giving the probability as a number of households instead of a fraction.
exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE O Level Paper 2 style

parts.prompt: Form an equation in x and solve it. Enter x.
How many households have a television only?
How many households have exactly one of the two appliances?
parts.explanation: Television only: 18; fridge only: 20 − 10 = 10. Total: 18 + 10 = 28. Check: 18 + 10 + 10 + 7 = 45.

parts.prompt: A household is chosen at random. What is the probability that it has a fridge but no television?
parts.explanation: Fridge only: 10 households out of 45, so $P = \frac{10}{45} = \frac{2}{9}$.

choices: The elements in both A and B
The elements in A or B
The elements in A but not in B
exercises.explanation: The intersection $A \cap B$ contains the elements common to both sets.

exercises.prompt: n(A) = 7, n(B) = 5 and $n(A \cap B)$ = 2. What is $n(A \cup B)$?
What is the complement A' of a set A?
choices: The elements of U that are not in A
The elements that are in A
The elements common to A and U
exercises.explanation: A' contains every element of the universal set U that is not in A.
Every element of A is already in B, so the elements common to A and B are exactly the elements of A.

exercises.prompt: V is the set of vowels in the word CAMEROON. What is n(V)?
exercises.explanation: The vowels are A, E, O and O, but an element is listed only once in a set: V = {A, E, O}, so n(V) = 3.
